title: Getting Started, Accounts and Trading Mechanics

submodules.title: 1. Ways to Participate: Direct Stocks vs Funds
submodules.intro: Should you buy one company or a whole basket?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WAYS TO PARTICIPATE
There is more than one door into the stock market. In this lesson you compare buying shares of single companies (direct stocks) with buying a basket through a fund. Bull Run uses simulated prices, not live NSE data, and nothing here is advice to buy anything.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A mutual fund works like a group lunch order. Many people put money into one common pot, and a professional fund manager picks the food (the holdings) for everyone. Your share of the pot is counted in units.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DIRECT STOCKS
When you buy a share, you own a tiny piece of that one business. You choose the company, how many shares, and when to buy or sell. Prices move all through market hours. Your result depends on that one company, so the risk is higher and you can lose part or even all of your money.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: FUNDS
• Mutual fund: pools money from many investors and spreads it across many companies or bonds. Its price is called NAV (Net Asset Value) and is usually worked out once a day after the market closes.
• ETF (Exchange Traded Fund): a basket that trades on the exchange like a share, with a live price during market hours.
• Funds charge a yearly fee (called an expense ratio). Fees quietly reduce your returns every year.
• Funds are spread out, but they are not safe. If the whole market falls, most funds fall too.

🧪 TRY IT: THE 50% DROP
Rohan has ₹1,000. Plan A: all of it in one company. Plan B: ₹50 each in 20 companies through a fund. Suppose one company falls by 50%.
Plan A loss: ₹500. Plan B loss: ₹25 (half of ₹50).
Now think: what if the whole market falls? Both plans can lose. Spreading out reduces single-company risk, not market risk.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Direct stocks put your result in one company's hands; funds spread it across many. Neither guarantees returns, and any real account must be opened and run by a parent or guardian.

quiz.question: What is a mutual fund?
options: One share of a single company
A pool of many investors' money managed by a professional and spread over many holdings
A savings account run by the government
A loan given by a broker
quiz.explanation: A mutual fund collects money from many people and a fund manager invests it across many holdings.

quiz.question: Rohan puts all his money in one company's shares. What is his main extra risk compared with a fund?
options: He will always pay more tax
His whole result depends on one company
quiz.explanation: With one company there is no spreading. If that company does badly, his whole investment suffers.

quiz.question: How is the price (NAV) of a regular mutual fund usually set?
options: Worked out once a day after the market closes
It changes every second like a share price
The bank fixes it for a year
quiz.explanation: A regular mutual fund's NAV is calculated once per day. ETFs are the ones that have live prices.

quiz.question: What is special about an ETF?
options: It can only be bought by people over 60
It trades on the exchange like a share during market hours
It pays a fixed interest rate
quiz.explanation: An ETF is a basket of holdings that is bought and sold on the exchange with a live price.

quiz.question: Which statement is true?
options: Both funds and direct stocks can lose value
Direct stocks are always safer than funds
quiz.explanation: Spreading money out lowers single-company risk, but no market investment is risk free.

submodules.title: 2. The Three Accounts: Bank, Trading, Demat
submodules.intro: Why do you need three accounts to own one share?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THREE ACCOUNTS, ONE SYSTEM
To buy a share in India, three accounts work together: a bank account, a trading account and a demat account. Think of them as three pipes in one water system. You met demat in Module 3. Now you will see how it fits with the other two.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Before demat, shares were printed paper certificates. They could be lost, torn, stolen or forged, and moving them took weeks. Today your shares are simply electronic records, safe from fire and thieves.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE BANK ACCOUNT
This is where your money lives. When you buy shares, money goes out of your bank account (through your trading account). When you sell, the money comes back to the same linked bank account. It must be in the same name as your other accounts.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE TRADING ACCOUNT
This is the doorway to the market. You log into your broker's app or website and place buy and sell orders here. It does not store your shares. It only sends your orders to the exchange.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE DEMAT ACCOUNT
This is the locker that holds your shares electronically. It is kept with a Depository Participant (DP), often your broker or a bank. Behind the DP sit two national depositories, NSDL and CDSL, which keep the official records of who owns what.

🧪 TRY IT: FOLLOW THE FLOW
Write down where things move when a parent buys 5 shares of a fictional company for ₹500 each:
1. ₹2,500 leaves the bank account.
2. The order is placed from the trading account.
3. The 5 shares arrive in the demat account.
Now reverse it for a sale. Where does the money end up?

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Bank holds money, trading account places orders, demat holds shares. For anyone under 18, a parent or guardian opens and operates these accounts.

quiz.question: Which account holds your shares electronically?
quiz.explanation: The demat account is the electronic locker where shares are stored.

quiz.question: Which account do you use to place buy and sell orders?
quiz.explanation: Orders are placed through the trading account on the broker's app or website.

quiz.question: Which organisations keep the official electronic records of share ownership in India?
quiz.explanation: NSDL and CDSL are the two depositories. Your DP connects you to them.

quiz.question: When shares are sold, where does the sale money finally go?
quiz.explanation: The sale money is paid out to your linked bank account.

quiz.question: Why is a demat account better than paper share certificates?
options: It is safer and faster, with no paper to lose or forge
quiz.explanation: Electronic records cannot be torn, burnt or easily forged, and transfers are quick.

submodules.title: 3. KYC and Account Opening
submodules.intro: What happens when a parent opens an account for you?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: KYC AND ACCOUNT OPENING
Before any broker lets someone invest, it must check who they are. This check is called KYC. This lesson explains it simply. As of 2026, in India people under 18 cannot sign financial contracts themselves, so a parent or guardian handles every step.

🤯 WOW FACT:
KYC records are stored with SEBI-registered KYC agencies, so once you are KYC verified, many other financial companies can often use that record. You usually do not repeat the full process every time.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT IS KYC?
KYC means Know Your Customer. It exists to stop people from using fake or stolen identities and to keep the market safe. Typical items include:
• PAN (Permanent Account Number)
• Proof of identity and address
• A photo and a signature
• Bank account proof
The exact documents and steps can change, so always check the broker's current list.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: UNDER-18 ACCOUNTS (AS OF 2026)
• A demat account can usually be opened in a minor's name, but a parent or legal guardian operates it until the child turns 18.
• The trading account stays in the guardian's name.
• Minors' accounts are limited. Risky activity such as intraday trading and futures and options is not allowed. Rules differ by broker, so ask them.
• At 18, the person completes fresh KYC and takes control.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STAY SAFE
• Use only SEBI-registered brokers.
• Never share your OTP, password or PIN with anyone, even someone who says they work for the broker.
• Nobody honest asks you to pay a 'fee' to release profits.

🧪 TRY IT: THE PARENT CHECKLIST
Make a list to discuss with a parent: PAN, address proof, bank details, mobile number linked to Aadhaar, email, and a recent photo. Which items do you think a broker needs for a child's account? Ask the broker to confirm.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
KYC proves who you are and keeps the market safe. Under 18, only a parent or guardian opens and operates accounts, and passwords and OTPs stay private.

quiz.question: What does KYC stand for?
quiz.explanation: KYC means Know Your Customer: a check of who the account holder really is.

quiz.question: Who opens and operates an investing account for someone under 18?
quiz.explanation: Minors cannot sign financial contracts, so a parent or legal guardian handles it.

quiz.question: A caller says he is from your broker and asks for your OTP. What should you do?
options: Share it if he sounds polite
Never share it and tell a parent
quiz.explanation: Brokers never need your OTP. Sharing it can let a fraudster take over the account.

quiz.question: What happens when a person with a minor's account turns 18?
options: They complete fresh KYC and take control
quiz.explanation: At 18 the person becomes an adult investor and completes KYC in their own name.

quiz.question: What is a sensible safety check before a family picks a broker?
options: Check that the broker is SEBI registered
Choose whoever offers a guaranteed return
Choose the one with the loudest ads
Pick the one a stranger recommends online
quiz.explanation: Only SEBI-registered brokers are allowed to do this work, and no one can guarantee returns.

submodules.title: 4. Choosing a Broker
submodules.intro: What should a family compare before picking a broker?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: CHOOSING A BROKER
A broker is the SEBI-registered company that carries your orders to the exchange. Families usually choose between two broad types: discount brokers and full-service brokers. This lesson shows what to compare. It does not recommend any company.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A broker earns brokerage and charges whether your trade makes a profit or a loss. That is why brokers talk so much about how often you trade, and why a calm, slow approach is usually kinder to your wallet.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: DISCOUNT vs FULL-SERVICE
• Discount broker: mostly app-based, low fees, you decide everything yourself. Fees can be a small flat amount per order, or even zero for some types of trades.
• Full-service broker: offers research, advice and a relationship manager, but usually charges more.
Neither type can promise profit. As of 2026, plans and prices change often, so check the current fee page.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT TO COMPARE
• Brokerage per order
• Account opening fee and yearly maintenance charge (AMC)
• DP charge when you sell shares
• App speed and reliability
• Customer support
• Learning material
• SEBI registration

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RED FLAGS
Walk away if someone promises guaranteed returns, sells secret tips, pushes you to borrow money, or pressures you to decide today.

🧪 TRY IT: FICTIONAL BROKER SHOWDOWN
Broker A charges ₹20 per order and no yearly fee. Broker B charges ₹0 per order but ₹300 yearly. A family expects 4 orders in a year.
Broker A: 4 x ₹20 = ₹80.
Broker B: ₹300.
Which is cheaper? What if they expected 40 orders? Always do the maths for your own use.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Compare fees, safety and support, not just advertising. Pick a SEBI-registered broker with a parent or guardian, and ignore anyone who promises guaranteed returns.

quiz.question: What is a discount broker usually known for?
options: Low fees and a mostly do-it-yourself, app-based service
Personal advice from a manager every day
quiz.explanation: Discount brokers keep costs low by offering mostly self-service apps.

quiz.question: What do full-service brokers typically offer?
options: Research and personal support, usually at higher cost
quiz.explanation: Full-service brokers add research and advice, and usually charge more for it.

quiz.question: Which of these is a clear red flag?
quiz.explanation: No one can guarantee market returns. Such a promise is a classic warning sign.

quiz.question: When does a broker collect brokerage?
options: On both winning and losing trades
quiz.explanation: Brokerage is a fee for carrying your order, so it is charged whatever the outcome.

quiz.question: In the TRY IT, a family places 4 orders. Broker A costs ₹20 per order, Broker B costs ₹300 yearly. Which is cheaper for 4 orders?
quiz.explanation: Broker A costs 4 x ₹20 = ₹80, much less than Broker B's ₹300.

submodules.title: 5. Reading a Stock Quote
submodules.intro: What do all those numbers on a stock screen mean?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: READING A STOCK QUOTE
A stock quote is the scoreboard of a share. At first it looks like a wall of numbers, but each one answers a simple question. The examples use a fictional company and made-up prices. Bull Run prices are simulated, never live NSE data.

🤯 WOW FACT:
At any moment a share has two prices, not one: the highest price buyers will pay (bid) and the lowest price sellers will accept (ask). The small gap between them is called the spread.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE PRICE NUMBERS
• LTP (Last Traded Price): the price of the most recent trade.
• Open: the first price of the day.
• High: the highest price traded today.
• Low: the lowest price traded today.
• Close (or previous close): the final price of the last session. Today's change is measured against it.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: VOLUME, BID AND ASK
• Volume: how many shares changed hands today. Higher volume usually means it is easier to buy and sell.
• Bid: the best price a buyer is offering.
• Ask (or offer): the best price a seller wants.
If you place a market buy, you generally pay near the ask. If you market sell, you generally get near the bid.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: A FICTIONAL QUOTE
Sunrise Foods Ltd (made up)
Previous close ₹99 | Open ₹100 | High ₹105 | Low ₹98 | LTP ₹103
Bid ₹102.95 | Ask ₹103.05 | Volume 2,50,000
The price is up ₹4 from the previous close.

🧪 TRY IT: CALCULATE THE CHANGE
Change % = (LTP - previous close) ÷ previous close x 100.
For Sunrise Foods: (103 - 99) ÷ 99 x 100 = about 4%.
Now try: previous close ₹200, LTP ₹210. What is the percentage change?

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A quote tells you where the price is now, where it has been today and how busy trading is. It never tells you where the price will go next.

quiz.question: What does LTP mean?
options: Lowest Trading Price of the year
quiz.explanation: LTP is the price at which the most recent trade happened.

quiz.question: What is the bid price?
options: The best price a buyer is offering
The best price a seller is asking
quiz.explanation: The bid is the highest price buyers are currently offering. The ask is the sellers' side.

quiz.question: What does volume show?
quiz.explanation: Volume counts the number of shares that changed hands.

quiz.question: What is a stock's 'High' for the day?
options: The price it will reach tomorrow
quiz.explanation: High is the top price reached so far in the day. It is history, not a prediction.

quiz.question: Previous close is ₹200 and LTP is ₹210. What is the percentage change?
quiz.explanation: The rise is ₹10 on ₹200, so 10 ÷ 200 x 100 = 5%.

submodules.title: 6. Order Types: Market, Limit, Stop-Loss
submodules.intro: Do you want a sure trade, or a sure price?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: ORDER TYPES
When you place an order, you tell the exchange how you want it done. The three basics are market, limit and stop-loss orders. Each gives you control over one thing and takes away control over another. All prices below are made up.

🤯 WOW FACT:
A market order means 'any price is fine'. In a fast-moving market, the price you actually get can be different from the price you saw a second earlier. This difference is often called slippage.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MARKET ORDER
A market order trades right away at the best available price. You are sure it will happen (if there are sellers or buyers), but you are not sure of the exact price. It can be costly in a thinly traded share or a jumpy market.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: LIMIT ORDER
You set the price. A limit buy says 'buy only at this price or lower'. A limit sell says 'sell only at this price or higher'. You control the price, but the order may never execute if the market does not reach it.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: STOP-LOSS ORDER
A stop-loss has a trigger price. When the price reaches the trigger, your sell order becomes active. It is designed to limit a loss. But it is not a magic shield: if a share suddenly drops far below your trigger, the sale can happen at a worse price than expected.

🧪 TRY IT: THREE SCENES
Bluewave Ltd (fictional) trades at ₹100.
1. A parent places a limit buy at ₹95. If the price stays above ₹95, what happens? The order waits and may not execute.
2. A market buy is placed. It executes at once near ₹100.
3. A parent holding bought shares at ₹100 sets a stop-loss trigger at ₹92. If the price falls to ₹92, the sell order activates.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Market orders give speed, limit orders give price control, and stop-loss orders help limit losses. None of them removes risk or guarantees a profit.

quiz.question: What does a market order guarantee?
options: That it will be executed (if the market has willing buyers or sellers)
quiz.explanation: A market order focuses on speed of execution, not on a fixed price.

quiz.question: A limit buy is set at ₹95 while the price is ₹100 and stays there. What happens?
options: It waits and may never execute
It turns into a market order
quiz.explanation: A limit buy will only trade at ₹95 or lower, so it waits until the price comes down.

quiz.question: What is a stop-loss order mainly designed to do?
options: Limit a possible loss when the price falls to a trigger
quiz.explanation: A stop-loss helps limit a loss, but it cannot stop prices from falling.

quiz.question: Which order type gives you control over the price you trade at?
quiz.explanation: With a limit order you name the price. The trade-off is that it may not execute.

quiz.question: A share suddenly drops far below your stop-loss trigger. What can happen?
options: The sale may happen at a worse price than the trigger
The order always executes at the trigger price exactly
quiz.explanation: In a sharp drop or gap, there may be no buyers at your trigger, so the exit price can be lower.

submodules.title: 7. The Life of an Order
submodules.intro: What really happens after you press Buy?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE LIFE OF AN ORDER
Pressing Buy is only the start of a short journey. An order is placed, sent, matched, executed and finally settled. Knowing these steps helps you understand statuses like Pending or Executed. You met T+1 in Module 3. Here you see where it fits.

🤯 WOW FACT:
The exchange's computers can match buyers and sellers in a tiny fraction of a second. Yet the final handover of shares and money (settlement) happens on the next working day.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: FIVE STEPS
1. Placed: your broker's app checks you have enough money (or shares to sell).
2. Sent: the order goes to the exchange and joins the order book.
3. Matched: a buyer and a seller who agree on a price are paired. The best price goes first. At the same price, the earlier order goes first.
4. Executed: the trade is done and you get a confirmation.
5. Settled: shares and money formally change hands.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: ORDER STATUS WORDS
• Pending or Open: waiting in the order book.
• Partially executed: only some of your shares have traded so far.
• Executed: fully done.
• Cancelled: removed by you or the system.
• Rejected: refused, often because of low funds or a wrong price.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: T+1 SETTLEMENT
As of 2026, regular share trades in India settle on T+1. That means the trade day (T) plus one working day. Weekends and exchange holidays do not count. After settlement the bought shares appear in your demat account, and money from a sale reaches your bank side.

🧪 TRY IT: COUNT THE DAYS
A parent buys shares on Tuesday. T+1 is Wednesday.
Shares bought on Friday: T+1 is Monday, as long as Monday is not a market holiday.
Find one more example using a holiday on a calendar.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
An order moves from placed to matched to executed to settled. Execution is quick, settlement follows on the next working day, and no step removes market risk.

quiz.question: Which of these happens first in the life of an order?
options: It is placed and checked by your broker's system
quiz.explanation: The order is placed first, then sent, matched, executed and settled.

quiz.question: Two buy orders arrive at the same price. Which goes first?
quiz.explanation: The exchange gives priority to the best price, and then to the earlier order.

quiz.question: What does T+1 mean (as of 2026)?
options: Trade day plus one working day
The same minute as the trade
quiz.explanation: Settlement takes place one working day after the trade day. Weekends and holidays are skipped.

quiz.question: A trade is made on Friday with no holidays coming. When does it settle on T+1?
quiz.explanation: Saturday and Sunday are not working days, so T+1 lands on Monday.

quiz.question: What does 'partially executed' mean?
options: Only some of the shares have traded so far
quiz.explanation: Part of the quantity has found a match, while the rest is still waiting.

submodules.title: 8. Costs and Charges
submodules.intro: Why is your profit smaller than the price difference?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: COSTS AND CHARGES
Every trade has small costs attached. Each one looks tiny, but together they can eat into your result. This lesson names them in simple words. As of 2026 the exact rates differ by broker and trade type and can change, so check the broker's current charges page. Rupee amounts here are made up.

🤯 WOW FACT:
If you buy a share and sell it at the exact same price, you still lose a little money because of charges. The price has to rise a bit just for you to break even.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE MAIN CHARGES
• Brokerage: the broker's fee for carrying out your order.
• STT (Securities Transaction Tax): a government tax charged on share trades.
• Exchange transaction charges: a small fee that goes to the exchange.
• SEBI turnover fee: a very small fee for the regulator.
• GST: tax charged on the broker's fee and some other charges.
• Stamp duty: a state-linked charge, usually on the buy side.
• DP charges: a fee the depository participant charges when shares are sold out of your demat account.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHERE TO SEE THEM
After trades, the broker sends a contract note. It lists every trade and every charge line by line. Many broker apps also have a brokerage calculator, so a family can estimate costs before trading. Read it each time.

🧪 TRY IT: FIND THE BREAK-EVEN
A parent buys 10 shares of a fictional company at ₹200 each. Assume all charges for buying and selling add up to ₹40.
Break-even rise per share = ₹40 ÷ 10 = ₹4.
So the sale price must be at least ₹204 just to get back to zero. Now try ₹60 of charges: what rise is needed?

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Costs are certain, while profits are not. Charges apply to winning and losing trades alike, so always know them before you trade.

quiz.question: Who receives the Securities Transaction Tax (STT)?
options: The company whose shares you bought
quiz.explanation: STT is a tax collected on share trades and paid to the government.

quiz.question: When is a DP charge usually applied?
options: Every time you open the app
When shares are sold out of the demat account
quiz.explanation: The depository participant charges a small fee when shares leave your demat account in a sale.

quiz.question: Which document lists every trade and every charge?
quiz.explanation: The contract note is the broker's detailed record of each trade and its charges.

quiz.question: In the TRY IT, 10 shares and total charges of ₹40. How much must the price rise per share just to break even?
quiz.explanation: ₹40 of charges spread over 10 shares is ₹4 per share.

quiz.question: Which statement is correct?
options: Charges apply only to winning trades
Charges apply to winning and losing trades
Only the broker pays the charges
quiz.explanation: Costs are charged on the trade itself, so they apply whether it ends in profit or loss.

submodules.title: 9. Taxes in Simple Terms
submodules.intro: When does the taxman want a share of your profit?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: TAXES IN SIMPLE TERMS
When shares are sold for a profit, that profit is called a capital gain, and the government may tax it. This lesson gives the basic idea only. Tax rules change often, so every number here is as of 2026 and must be checked with a parent or a tax professional. This is not tax advice.

🤯 WOW FACT:
You normally pay capital gains tax only when you sell. A share that has gone up on screen but is still unsold is a paper gain, and a paper gain can disappear again.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CAPITAL GAIN
Capital gain = selling price - buying price (counting the costs). If the result is below zero, it is a capital loss. Losses can sometimes be used to reduce tax on gains, but the rules are detailed, so ask a professional.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: SHORT-TERM vs LONG-TERM (AS OF 2026)
For listed shares, the holding period decides the type:
• Held 12 months or less: short-term capital gain, taxed at 20% (as of 2026).
• Held more than 12 months: long-term capital gain, taxed at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh in a financial year (as of 2026). Smaller long-term gains in that year are not taxed.
These figures may change in future Budgets. Check the latest before relying on them.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: CHILDREN AND TAX
Income earned in a minor's name is usually added to a parent's income for tax. The family should ask a tax professional how this applies to them. Dividends and fund gains can have their own rules too.

🧪 TRY IT: TWO FICTIONAL SALES
Isha's family sells shares held for 8 months with a gain of ₹10,000. Using the 20% short-term rate above: ₹10,000 x 20% = ₹2,000 tax.
Another family sells shares held for 15 months with a gain of ₹60,000 and has no other long-term gains that year. That is under the ₹1.25 lakh limit, so no long-term tax applies under the rule above.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Tax depends on profit and holding period. Rules and rates change, so always check the latest and ask a parent or tax professional. Tax never makes a loss disappear, and no return is guaranteed.

quiz.question: What is a capital gain?
options: A bank's interest on a loan
A fee paid to the broker
The profit from selling an asset for more than you paid
quiz.explanation: A capital gain is the profit made when an asset is sold above its purchase price.

quiz.question: As of 2026, for listed shares, what holding period counts as short-term?
quiz.explanation: Listed shares held for 12 months or less produce short-term gains (as of 2026).

quiz.question: As of 2026, what is the short-term capital gains tax rate on listed shares used in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson uses 20% (as of 2026). Rates can change, so always check the latest.

quiz.question: Using the lesson's 20% rate, what is the tax on a short-term gain of ₹10,000?
What is the smartest step if a family is unsure how tax applies to them?
options: Ask a parent or a tax professional and check current rules
quiz.explanation: Rules change and depend on each person's case, so check the latest and ask a qualified person.

submodules.title: 10. Trading Hours, Sessions and Market Holidays
submodules.intro: When can you actually trade, and why does timing matter?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: WHEN THE MARKET OPENS
The stock market is not open all day and night. It follows a timetable, and knowing it helps you understand why prices sometimes jump at the open. As of 2026 the main times below apply to the NSE and BSE equity markets, but exchanges can tweak sessions, so check their official sites.

🤯 WOW FACT:
The exchanges are normally closed on weekends, yet they sometimes hold special sessions. A Sunday session was held on Budget Day in 2026, and a short Muhurat session is held around Diwali.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE DAILY TIMETABLE (AS OF 2026)
• Pre-open session: about 9:00 to 9:15 AM. Orders are collected so an opening price can be fixed.
• Regular session: 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM, Monday to Friday.
• After 3:30 PM: closing price is worked out, and short closing or post-close sessions may follow. Details have changed in 2026, so check the exchange.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: HOLIDAYS
The market is closed on Saturdays, Sundays and exchange-declared holidays. The list for each year is published on the NSE and BSE websites. Remember T+1 counts only working days, so a holiday can delay settlement.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: ORDERS OUTSIDE HOURS
Some brokers allow after-market orders (AMO). They wait in a queue and go to the exchange in the next session. The market can open higher or lower than the last close, so the price you expected may not be the price you get. This is called a gap. Price bands from Module 3 can also pause moves during the day.

🧪 TRY IT: PLAN A WEEK
Open the official holiday list with a parent. Count how many trading days there are in this month. Then answer: if a parent places an after-market order on Sunday evening, when will it first reach the exchange?

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Regular trading runs 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM on working weekdays (as of 2026). Always check official exchange sources for holidays and changes, and remember that overnight prices can gap.

quiz.question: As of 2026, what are the regular equity trading hours on the NSE and BSE?
options: 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM, Monday to Friday
quiz.explanation: The main equity session runs from 9:15 AM to 3:30 PM on working weekdays.

quiz.question: On which days is the regular market normally closed?
quiz.explanation: The market is closed on weekends and on holidays declared by the exchange.

quiz.question: What happens to an after-market order (AMO)?
options: It is always filled at last night's price
It waits and goes to the exchange in the next session
quiz.explanation: An AMO is queued and sent when the market next opens, and the price may differ from before.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of the pre-open session?
options: To collect orders so an opening price can be set
quiz.explanation: Orders gathered between roughly 9:00 and 9:15 AM help fix the opening price.

quiz.question: Where should a family check the market holiday list and any timing changes?
options: The official NSE and BSE websites
quiz.explanation: Official exchange sources are the reliable place for current dates and timings.

submodules.title: 11. Case Study: One Trade, Start to Finish
submodules.intro: What does one full trade look like, with every cost?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: FOLLOW ONE TRADE
Kavya, 16, watches while her father, Mr. Nair, shows her one trade in his own adult account. The company, prices and charges are all made up to teach the steps. They are not real rates and not a suggestion to buy anything.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Even a small ₹2,000 trade has several different charge lines on its contract note. A trade can feel simple, yet it has a lot of tiny moving parts.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE BUY
Mr. Nair decides to buy 10 shares of a fictional firm, Mangal Tea Ltd. The last price is ₹203. He places a limit buy order at ₹200, valid for the day.
• 10:05 AM: order placed, status Pending (price still above ₹200).
• 10:40 AM: the price dips to ₹200 and the order executes.
• Share cost: 10 x ₹200 = ₹2,000.
• Assumed charges: ₹12.
• Total paid: ₹2,012.
On the next working day (T+1), the 10 shares appear in his demat account.

🍕 MINI CASE: THE SELL
Three months later, he places a limit sell at ₹230 and it executes.
• Sale value: 10 x ₹230 = ₹2,300.
• Assumed charges (including a DP charge): ₹14.
• Money received: ₹2,286.
• Profit after charges: ₹2,286 - ₹2,012 = ₹274.
He held for under 12 months, so it is a short-term gain. Using 20% (as of 2026), tax would be about ₹55, leaving roughly ₹219. The family should confirm tax with a professional.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: WHAT IF IT HAD GONE WRONG?
Suppose the sale had been at ₹190 with the same ₹14 charges: 10 x ₹190 = ₹1,900 - ₹14 = ₹1,886. Compared with ₹2,012 paid, that is a loss of ₹126. Losses are real, and charges apply either way.

🧪 TRY IT: DO YOUR OWN MATH
A fictional trade: buy 5 shares at ₹400 with ₹8 charges, sell at ₹420 with ₹9 charges. What is the profit after charges?
(Answer: buy cost ₹2,008, sale money ₹2,091, profit ₹83.)

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
A full trade has an order, an execution, T+1 settlement, charges and possibly tax. Winning or losing, the steps are the same, and nothing is guaranteed.

quiz.question: Which order type did Mr. Nair use to buy?
quiz.explanation: He set the price himself at ₹200, so it was a limit order.

quiz.question: What was the total amount paid for the 10 shares, including charges?
quiz.explanation: ₹2,000 for the shares plus ₹12 of charges gives ₹2,012.

quiz.question: When did the bought shares appear in the demat account?
quiz.explanation: Under T+1, settlement happens one working day after the trade.

quiz.question: After the sale at ₹230 and ₹14 of charges, what was the profit after charges?
quiz.explanation: He received ₹2,286 and paid ₹2,012, so the profit was ₹274.

quiz.question: If the shares had been sold at ₹190 with the same ₹14 charges, what would the result be?
quiz.explanation: The sale gives ₹1,886 against ₹2,012 paid, which is a loss of ₹126.

submodules.title: 12. Module Recap: Common Beginner Mistakes
submodules.intro: How do you put it all together and avoid the usual traps?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: PUTTING IT ALL TOGETHER
You now know the pipes, the paperwork, the numbers and the costs. This final lesson ties them into one picture and flags the mistakes beginners make most often. Remember: Bull Run uses simulated prices and is for learning only.

🤯 WOW FACT:
Studies by SEBI, India's market regulator, have found that a large majority of individual traders in futures and options lost money. Risky, fast trading is where beginners get hurt the most.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE BIG PICTURE
1. A parent or guardian opens and operates real accounts for anyone under 18.
2. Three accounts work together: bank, trading and demat.
3. Choose a SEBI-registered broker after comparing fees.
4. Read the quote: LTP, high, low, volume, bid and ask.
5. Pick the right order type: market, limit or stop-loss.
6. Know the order journey and T+1 settlement.
7. Count the costs and the tax before you trade.
8. Check the trading hours and holidays.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: COMMON BEGINNER MISTAKES
• Borrowing money to trade. Debt makes losses bigger and harder to survive.
• Following social media tips or 'guaranteed return' promises.
• Putting all money in one company.
• Ignoring charges and tax.
• Using market orders in jumpy markets.
• Trading with money needed for fees, food or school.
• Sharing OTPs or passwords.
• Panic selling after one bad day.

🧪 TRY IT: THE PRE-TRADE CHECK
Before every simulator trade, answer five questions in writing:
1. Why am I making this trade?
2. How much could I lose, and can I accept that?
3. Which order type fits, and why?
4. What will the costs be?
5. When and why would I exit?
If you cannot answer all five, do not trade yet.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Good trading habits start with safety, patience and knowing the costs. Never borrow to trade, never trust guaranteed returns, and always involve a parent or guardian for anything real.

quiz.question: Which money is appropriate to put into the market (with a guardian's involvement)?
options: Only money that can be risked without hurting daily life
quiz.explanation: Markets can fall, so only spare money that is not needed for essentials should ever be at risk.

quiz.question: Why is borrowing money to trade dangerous?
options: Debt makes losses bigger and still has to be repaid
quiz.explanation: If a trade loses, the loan still has to be repaid, so the damage grows.

quiz.question: A stranger messages you offering 'guaranteed returns' on a stock. What is this most likely?
quiz.explanation: No one can guarantee market returns. Such promises are common in scams.

quiz.question: What is the first step before any real account is opened for a person under 18?
options: A parent or guardian takes charge and completes the process
Share the OTP with a friend
quiz.explanation: Under 18, a parent or guardian opens and operates the accounts.

quiz.question: What kind of prices does the Bull Run simulator use?
quiz.explanation: Bull Run prices are simulated and are never live NSE data.
